newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Jailed Timor leader would reject any exile deal.
newsitem.headline: Jailed Timor leader would reject any exile deal.

text.p: Jailed East Timor guerrilla leader Xanana Gusmao would reject any freedom deal involving his exile from the Indonesian-controlled territory, his spokesman, Nobel laureate Jose Ramos Horta said on Monday.
Ramos Horta told the Portuguese news agency Lusa that self-determination remained the principal demand of his movement, which is opposed to Indonesia's 1976 annexation of the Pacific territory.

The Nobel laureate, who was jointly awarded the 1996 Peace Prize with East Timor bishop Carlos Belo, spoke to Lusa in the former Portuguese African colony of Cape Verde. He travelled there from South Africa where he met President Nelson Mandela.

His trip to Pretoria, at Mandela's request, stirred speculation in Portugal that the South African leader might be seeking to mediate between Portugal, which backs the resistance movement's demands, and Indonesia.

On a visit to Indonesa this month, Mandela secured the temporary release of Gusmao from Jakarta's notorious Cipinang jail to dine with him at the government guest house beside President Suharto's palace.
The Portuguese newspaper Expresso reported last weekend that Mandela had urged Jakarta to free Gusmao, who is serving a 20-year jail sentence for resisting Indonesian rule.
News that Mandela had invited Portuguese President Jorge Sampaio to visit South Africa to discuss Timor further stoked talk that some sort of deal might be in the offing.
Ramos Horta said that the possibility of a "conditional" release for Gusmao had not been raised in his talks with Mandela and was in any case unacceptable.
"Xanana will not accept any conditional release involving exile," he was quoted as saying by Lusa.
Portugal and Indonesia have been meeting periodically under U.N. auspices in an attempt to agree on the future of the territory where a small guerrilla force is still active.

Indonesia invaded East Timor, 500 km (300 miles) northwest of Australia, in 1975 when the Portuguese left and annexed it one year later. The annexation has never been recognised by the United Nations.
